section.title: Inverse trigonometric functions
section.p: An inverse function reverses input and output. But sine and cosine repeat, so they do not have inverses on the whole real line.
If we tried to invert sine on all real numbers, the output 0 would have many possible inputs. That is not a function.
The repair is familiar: restrict the domain before taking the inverse.

subsection.title: Why restrictions are needed
subsection.p: A function has an inverse only when it is one-to-one on the domain we choose.

On that interval, it increases from -1 to 1. So we define \arcsin x as the inverse of sine on this restricted interval.

note.title: Arcsine
note.p: Thus \arcsin x is the angle in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right] whose sine is x.

subsection.p: The range condition is part of the definition.
The angle \frac{5\pi}{6} is not in the chosen range for arcsine.
